newsitem.title: USA: U.S. budget agreement follows years of wrangling.
newsitem.headline: U.S. budget agreement follows years of wrangling.

text.p: The historic tentative agreement reached on Monday to balance the U.S. budget by 2002 followed years of wrangling between President Bill Clinton and congressional Republicans over taxing and spending priorities.

-- 1992: Democrat Clinton defeats incumbent Republican President George Bush on a promise to improve the economy. One of Clinton's campaign promises is a tax cut for the middle class. But the U.S. budget deficit balloons to $290.4 billion in fiscal year ended September 1992.

-- 1993: Clinton, faced with the worsening budget deficit, abandons his middle-class tax cut pledge and proposes budget deficit that raises taxes instead. Congress approves the plan with not a single Republican vote, and Republicans vow to seek retribution at the polls.

-- 1994: Republicans score sweeping victory in congressional elections, winning majority control of both the Senate and House of Represenatives for first time in 40 years on a "Contract with America" platform promising to reduce the size of government and cut taxes.

-- 1995: Republicans propose major tax and spending plan as a blueprint for balancing the budget by 2002. The proposal included a $245 billion tax cut, a plan to drastically slow the growth of many popular programmes including Medicaid and Medicare health benefits for elderly and poor Americans and a proposal to end a 60-year-old guarantee of federal aid for poor children, substituting lump-sum cash payments to states.

They try to force Clinton to agree to the cuts by shutting down the government in November 1995, then a second time Dec. 16 through Jan. 6, 1996. Clinton refuses to budge, vetoing the Republican plan. Voters blame Republicans more than Clinton for the government shutdown.

-- November 1996: Clinton re-elected to a second term as president over former Republican Senate leader Bob Dole. But voters also return Republican majorities to Congress. Chastened by their battles, Clinton and Republicans vow after the election to try again to work together.

-- May 16, 1997: After months of negotiations, Clinton and congressional Republicans agree on the outlines of a deal to balance the budget by 2002. It includes spending for Clinton's priorities of health, education and the environment, while cutting taxes as Republicans wanted. Work starts in Congress to write legislation to implement the agreement.

-- July 28, 1997: Clinton and Republican leaders of Congress agree on the details of the legislation to implement the spending and tax cuts. Agreement comes as figures show U.S. budget already close to balance. Latest data show the U.S. budget deficit fell to $11 billion in first nine months of fiscal 1997.
